newsitem.title: GERMANY: Poll shows most Germans against single currency - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows most Germans against single currency - newspaper.

text.p: A majority of Germans opppose the planned single European currency championed by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, an opinion poll showed over the weekend.

The Infratest Burke financial research institute found in a poll that 37 percent of Germans welcomed the plans for a single currency while 57 percent were against it, the Welt am Sonntag newspaper reported on Saturday.

The poll showed seven out of 10 citizens thought the planned European economic and monetary union (EMU), which is due to start in 1999, would go forward though only 40 percent thought Germany would meet the conditions needed to take part.

Of those against the plan, most were worried that the planned currency, the euro, would be weaker or less stable than the German mark, while others feared that Germany would end up carrying the financial burden of the economic plan.
The newspaper said 700 citizens from the states of the former West Germany had taken part in the poll, which was conducted at the end of last year.
Since then, doubts have grown about Germany's ability to qualify for the single currency.

The respected weekly magazine Der Spiegel said the government itself sees a risk that Germany's 1997 budget deficit may rise more than expected beyond the ceiling allowed for joining the single currency.

Internal calculations at the Chancellor's office showed the budget deficit climbing as high as 4.15 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, the magazine said in a statement ahead of publication on Monday.

A German government spokesman denied the report, saying the Chancellor's office had not made such calculations. The figure is well above the 3 percent level mandated by the Maastricht Treaty for joining the single currency and is also above the government's official target of 2.9 percent.
Meanwhile, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Sunday that the European Union was beyond turning back on its march to a single currency.
"I think we have reached the point of no return on the way to the euro," Kinkel told reporters in the Netherlands at an informal meeting of European Union foreign ministers.
